subject: predict() help to estimate abundance using a robust n-mixture design

messages.subject: predict() help to estimate abundance using a robust n-mixture design
parts:
Hi all, 


This google group has been incredibly informative and helpful! Thank you to everyone who has taken the time to keep this group running for more than a decade! As a disclaimer, I have seen other posts similar to this question I will introduce, but with small yet crucial differences, so I thought it was still worth posting this question. 


I am doing a robust N-mixture analysis for a salamander species across 5 primary periods. Within each primary period, there are 4 secondary periods. Being a robust model, I used 'unmarkedFrameGPC' to create my unmarked object and 'gpcount' to fit the models for lambda, phi, and p. 


This is the setup for gpcount(): 

gpcount(lambda, phi, p, data, mixture, K)


This is my top model: 

mod.5 = gpcount(~AvgCrevCt, ~yr.site.covs, ~temp, gs.umf, mixture = "NB", K = 100)


Where, 

AvgCrevCt is the average total number of crevices in a given rock outcrop; continuous

yr.site.covs is the season the primary period fell within; categorical (warm1, cool1, warm2, cool2, warm3)

temp is temperature; continuous


I am trying to predict the population sizes for each of my 19 sites while accounting for (1) the varying occupancy (phi) in the studied area versus the super-population based on season, and (2) the imperfect detection probability (p) based on temperature. However, I am struggling to achieve this with the predict() function. 


Based on other posts in this Google group (https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/M0EW6V2xZEU; https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/5UnUR4Ui4wA), 

I have made a new dataframe that spans the range of my scaled covariate data: 


topmod.newdata = data.frame(temp = seq(-2.76,1.54,length = 19), 

                           AvgCrevCt = seq(-1.24,2.99, length = 19),

                           yr.site.covs = factor("C1", levels = c("C1","C2","W1","W2","W3")))



And then I implement the predict() function using that new data and the top model, mod.5. 


topmod.pred = predict(mod.5, type = "lambda", newdata = topmod.newdata, appendData = TRUE)


The output is not what I was hoping to achieve... but is admittedly logical based on the newdata I fed it. This shows the predicted abundance for each temperature and average crevice count throughout the range of each covariate.

Alternatively, I have also tried to brute-force it without creating a new dataframe. My thinking was the top model (mod.5) only included the relevant covariates anyways: 


test.pred = predict(type = “lambda”, mod.5) 


and I received the following output:

This output looks more likely to be site-specific population sizes, but I'm hesitant to assume so. These estimates are a bit higher than I would expect; however, it is using a negative binomial distribution which tends to inflate estimations.


Is this last bit of code really the site-specific population sizes even though I did not create a new dataframe for the top-ranked variables? If not, can anyone help point me in the right direction?


Respectfully,

Megan

Megan,

I don't think I have an answer for you, but I'll attempt to clarify the question so that one of the more knowledgeable unmarked gurus can swoop in and correct me.  (I echo your thanks to those to contribute, and whose knowledge is well beyond mine!).

It seems like you're trying to answer a question across multiple dimensions at once, i.e., at different sites during different seasons and with varying detection covariable values (temperature), all in one data frame.  My understanding is that because the new data frame for predict is only a table in two dimensions, you can't vary more than one thing at a time.  So, I believe you can set up a data frame to examine differences in your 19 sites at a set temperature during a set season.  Or, you can look at the average across your sites at a set temperature during various seasons.  Or, you could look at the effect of temperature during a given season at an 'average' or one particular site.  I don't think you can do all at once, but by predicting and then graphing these predictions, varying one variable at a time, you can get a sense of the relationships.  And note that you could choose an average, or a meaningful value (we will only survey at temperatures above X value, so set temp as X in the predict dataframe and then estimate N across all sites), or any of the seasons.  It seems like unmarked is predicting across 3 variables at once, which might be mathematically correct but is very hard to interpret meaningfully.

Is that the crux of the issue, or do I misunderstand the question?

-Alex
